chapters.title: Day 1: Introduction to Python and Setup

body.text: Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language known for its simple, readable syntax. It is used for web development, data analysis, automation, artificial intelligence, scientific computing and more.

items: Easy to read and write
Interpreted language
Free and open source
Huge standard library
Cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux)

body.text: Python was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991.
Python can be downloaded from python.org. During installation on Windows, make sure to check the option 'Add Python to PATH' so it can be run from any terminal.

rows: Usually pre-installed; use apt or dnf

items: IDLE (comes bundled with Python)
VS Code (lightweight, extensible)
PyCharm (full-featured IDE)
Jupyter Notebook (great for data work)

body.text: The print() function displays output on the screen. It is usually the first command every beginner learns.

body.code: print("Hello, World!")

items: Run a script file: python filename.py
Use the interactive shell (REPL): type python in a terminal
Run cells inside Jupyter Notebook

body.text: Comments are notes in code that Python ignores when running. They help explain what the code does.

body.code:
# This is a single line comment
"""
This is a
multi-line comment
"""
print("Comments do not run")

body.text: Good comments make code easier to read and maintain, but too many unnecessary comments can clutter code.

questions.question: Who created the Python programming language?
questions.explanation: Python was created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991.

questions.question: Which function is used to display output in Python?
questions.explanation: The print() function outputs text or values to the screen.

questions.question: Which symbol is used to write a single-line comment in Python?
questions.explanation: The # symbol marks the rest of the line as a comment.

questions.question: Python is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Python code is executed by an interpreter and is considered high-level and readable.

questions.question: What is used to run a Python script from the terminal?
questions.explanation: A script is executed using the command 'python filename.py'.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid Python file extension?
questions.explanation: Python script files use the .py extension.

questions.question: Which tool comes bundled with the standard Python installation?
questions.explanation: IDLE is the default editor that ships with Python.

questions.question: Why should you add Python to PATH during Windows installation?
options: So Python can be run from any terminal location
questions.explanation: Adding Python to PATH lets you invoke it from any command prompt location.

body.text: A variable is a name used to store a value in memory. In Python, you do not need to declare a type; it is assigned automatically based on the value.

body.code:
name = "Alice"
age = 25
height = 5.6
is_student = True

items: Must start with a letter or underscore
Cannot start with a number
Can contain letters, numbers and underscores
Case-sensitive (age and Age are different)
Cannot use Python keywords like if, for, class

body.text: The type() function returns the data type of a variable.

body.code:
x = 10
print(type(x))   # <class 'int'>

body.text: Python allows converting one data type into another using built-in functions such as int(), float(), str() and bool().

body.code:
a = "10"
b = int(a)      # converts string to int
c = float(b)    # converts int to float
d = str(c)      # converts float to string

body.text: Python variables are dynamically typed, meaning the same variable can hold different types at different times.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid Python variable name?
questions.explanation: A variable name can start with an underscore, but not a digit, hyphen, or reserved keyword.

questions.question: What data type is the value 3.14 in Python?
questions.explanation: Decimal numbers are represented as the float data type.

questions.question: Which function is used to check the data type of a variable?
questions.explanation: type() returns the data type of the given value.

questions.question: What will int("25") return?
questions.explanation: int() converts a numeric string into an integer value.

questions.question: Which of the following is a boolean value in Python?
questions.explanation: True and False (without quotes) are Python's boolean literals.

questions.question: Is Python a statically typed or dynamically typed language?
questions.explanation: Python determines variable types at runtime, making it dynamically typed.

questions.question: What does the statement x = y = 5 do?
options: Assigns 5 to both x and y
questions.explanation: Chained assignment assigns the same value to multiple variables at once.

questions.question: Which naming rule is correct for Python variables?
options: Variable names can start with a digit
Variable names cannot be Python keywords
questions.explanation: Reserved keywords like if, for, and class cannot be used as variable names.

body.text: Operators are special symbols used to perform operations on values and variables, such as arithmetic calculations or comparisons.

body.code:
print(5 == 5)   # True
print(5 != 3)   # True

rows: True if both conditions are True
True if at least one condition is True

body.code:
a = 10
print(a > 5 and a < 20)  # True

body.text: When multiple operators appear in one expression, Python follows an order of precedence: parentheses first, then exponents, then multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction.

body.code: result = 2 + 3 * 4   # 14, not 20, because * runs before +

questions.question: What is the result of 10 // 3 in Python?
questions.explanation: Floor division // discards the decimal part and returns 3.

questions.question: What does the % operator return?
questions.explanation: The modulus operator % returns the remainder of a division.

questions.question: Which operator is used to check equality between two values?
questions.explanation: == compares two values for equality; = is used for assignment.

questions.question: What is the output of 2 ** 3?
questions.explanation: ** is the exponent operator, so 2 ** 3 equals 8.

questions.question: Which logical operator returns True only if both conditions are True?
questions.explanation: The and operator requires both conditions to be True.

questions.question: What does x += 5 do?
options: Adds 5 to x and reassigns it
questions.explanation: x += 5 is shorthand for x = x + 5.

questions.question: According to operator precedence, what is 4 + 2 * 3?
questions.explanation: Multiplication is evaluated before addition, giving 4 + 6 = 10.

questions.question: Which operator reverses a boolean result?
questions.explanation: The not operator inverts True to False and vice versa.

chapters.title: Day 4: Input, Output and String Formatting

body.text: The input() function allows a program to accept data typed by the user. It always returns the value as a string.

body.code:
name = input("Enter your name: ")
print("Hello,", name)

body.text: Since input() always returns a string, numeric input must be converted using int() or float().

body.code:
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
print(age + 1)

rows: What to print at the end (default is newline)

body.code:
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")   # a-b-c
print("Hello", end="!")          # Hello! (no new line)

items: f-strings (recommended, Python 3.6+)
str.format() method
% formatting (older style)

body.code:
name = "Sam"
age = 20
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
print("{} is {} years old".format(name, age))
print("%s is %d years old" % (name, age))

body.text: f-strings are the most modern and readable way to format strings in Python.

questions.question: What data type does input() always return?
questions.explanation: input() always returns the entered data as a string, regardless of what was typed.

questions.question: How would you convert user input into an integer?
questions.explanation: int() converts the string returned by input() into an integer.

questions.question: Which print() parameter controls what appears between multiple printed values?
questions.explanation: The sep parameter defines the separator placed between printed items.

questions.question: Which is the modern, recommended way to format strings in Python 3.6+?
questions.explanation: f-strings offer a concise and readable way to embed expressions in strings.

questions.question: What does f"{pi:.2f}" do if pi = 3.14159?
questions.explanation: The .2f format spec rounds a float to 2 decimal places.

questions.question: What does print("Hi", end="!") output?
options: Hi followed by a new line
questions.explanation: The end parameter replaces the default newline with the given string, here '!'.

questions.question: Which function displays a prompt and waits for the user to type a value?
questions.explanation: input() displays an optional prompt and waits for user input.

questions.question: What will "{} is {}".format("Tom", 5) output?
questions.explanation: str.format() substitutes the placeholders {} with the given arguments in order.

body.text: Conditional statements let a program make decisions and execute different code depending on whether a condition is True or False.
Python uses indentation (usually 4 spaces) instead of curly braces to define blocks of code.

body.code:
age = 20
status = "Adult" if age >= 18 else "Minor"
print(status)

items: Forgetting the colon (:) at the end of if/elif/else
Inconsistent indentation
Using = instead of == for comparison

questions.question: What symbol does Python require at the end of an if statement?
questions.explanation: Python requires a colon at the end of if, elif, and else statements.

questions.question: How does Python define a block of code inside an if statement?
questions.explanation: Python uses consistent indentation instead of braces to group statements.

questions.question: Which keyword checks an additional condition after an if statement fails?
questions.explanation: elif is Python's keyword for checking another condition.

questions.question: What is the output of: x = 10; print('Even') if x % 2 == 0 else print('Odd')
questions.explanation: 10 % 2 equals 0, so the condition is True and 'Even' is printed.

questions.question: In an if-elif-else chain, how many blocks execute at most?
questions.explanation: Python evaluates conditions in order and executes only the first True block.

questions.question: What mistake does this code contain? if x = 5:
questions.explanation: A single = is assignment; comparisons require ==, otherwise Python raises a syntax error.

questions.question: What does a nested if statement mean?
options: An if statement with no condition
An if statement placed inside another if statement
questions.explanation: A nested if is an if statement written inside the body of another if statement.

questions.question: What is the short-hand (ternary) form of if-else used for?
options: Writing a simple conditional expression in one line
questions.explanation: The ternary operator lets you write value_if_true if condition else value_if_false in a single line.

concept.title: Loops in Python: for and while

body.text: A loop is used to repeat a block of code multiple times, which avoids writing the same statement over and over.
A for loop iterates over a sequence such as a list, string, or range of numbers.

body.code:
for i in range(5):
    print(i)   # prints 0 1 2 3 4

body.text: 4. Looping Through a String or List
A while loop repeats a block of code as long as a given condition remains True.

body.code:
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1

body.text: Always ensure the condition in a while loop eventually becomes False, otherwise it creates an infinite loop.

rows: Best when number of iterations is known
Best when repetition depends on a condition

questions.question: What does range(5) generate?
questions.explanation: range(5) produces numbers from 0 up to, but not including, 5.

questions.question: Which loop is best when the exact number of repetitions is known in advance?
questions.explanation: A for loop is well-suited to iterating a known number of times or over a sequence.

questions.question: What will range(0, 10, 2) generate?
questions.explanation: The third argument in range() is the step, so it produces even numbers 0 to 8.

questions.question: What could cause an infinite while loop?
questions.explanation: If the loop's condition never evaluates to False, the while loop will run forever.

questions.question: What does this loop print? for ch in "Hi": print(ch)
options: H then i on separate lines
questions.explanation: Iterating over a string yields each character individually, printed on its own line.

questions.question: Which statement about while loops is correct?
options: They repeat as long as the condition is True
They cannot use a counter variable
questions.explanation: A while loop continues executing its block as long as its condition remains True.

questions.question: What is the purpose of count += 1 inside a while loop counting example?
options: To increment the counter and eventually stop the loop
questions.explanation: Incrementing the counter changes the condition over time so the loop can end.

questions.question: Which of the following can a for loop iterate over?
options: Sequences like lists, strings, and ranges
questions.explanation: A for loop can iterate over any iterable, including lists, strings, tuples, and ranges.

chapters.title: Day 7: Loop Control and Nested Loops

concept.title: Loop Control Statements and Nested Loops

body.text: break immediately stops the loop, even if the loop condition is still True.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.
pass does nothing; it is used as a placeholder when a statement is syntactically required but no action is needed yet.
A nested loop is a loop placed inside another loop. The inner loop completes all its iterations for each single iteration of the outer loop.
Python allows an else block after a loop, which runs only if the loop completes without hitting a break.

items: break: search and stop once found
continue: skip invalid or unwanted values
pass: placeholder in incomplete code
Nested loops: patterns, grids, multiplication tables

questions.question: What does the break statement do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: break terminates the loop entirely, regardless of the loop condition.

questions.question: What does the continue statement do?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and continues with the next
questions.explanation: continue skips the remaining code in the current iteration and moves to the next one.

questions.question: When is the pass statement used?
options: As a placeholder where code is syntactically required but not yet written
questions.explanation: pass is a null operation used to satisfy syntax without executing any action.

questions.question: What is a nested loop?
options: A loop placed inside another loop
questions.explanation: A nested loop is one loop written inside the body of another loop.

questions.question: In the code: for i in range(3): for j in range(2): print(i,j) — how many times does print() execute?
questions.explanation: The outer loop runs 3 times and the inner loop runs 2 times each, giving 3 x 2 = 6 total executions.

questions.question: When does the else clause attached to a for loop execute?
options: Only if the loop completes without break
questions.explanation: The else block on a loop runs only when the loop finishes all iterations without hitting break.

questions.question: What is printed by: for i in range(4): if i==2: continue; print(i)
questions.explanation: When i equals 2, continue skips printing that value, so 0, 1, 3 are printed.

questions.question: Which statement would you use to stop searching a list once a target value is found?
questions.explanation: break immediately exits the loop once the desired condition (e.g., value found) is met.

body.text: A string is a sequence of characters enclosed in single, double, or triple quotes, used to represent text.

body.code:
s1 = 'Hello'
s2 = "World"
s3 = '''Multi
line
string'''

body.text: Each character in a string has an index starting from 0. Negative indexing counts from the end.

body.code:
s = "Python"
print(s[0])     # P
print(s[-1])    # n
print(s[1:4])   # yth

a = "Hello" + " " + "World"
b = "Hi" * 3   # HiHiHi

s = "Python3"
print(s.isalpha())    # False (has a digit)
print(s.isdigit())    # False
print(s.isalnum())    # True

body.text: Strings in Python are immutable — methods like upper() and replace() return a new string rather than modifying the original.

questions.question: What is the index of the first character in a Python string?
questions.explanation: Python uses zero-based indexing, so the first character is at index 0.

questions.question: What does 'Python'[-1] return?
questions.explanation: Negative index -1 refers to the last character of the string, which is 'n'.

questions.question: Which method converts a string to uppercase?
questions.explanation: The upper() method returns a new string with all characters in uppercase.

questions.question: What does 'Hi' * 3 produce?
questions.explanation: The * operator repeats a string the given number of times without adding spaces.

questions.question: Which method splits a string into a list based on a delimiter?
questions.explanation: split() breaks a string into a list of substrings using the given separator.

questions.question: Are strings in Python mutable or immutable?
questions.explanation: Once created, a string's contents cannot be changed in place; operations return new strings.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.find('l') return?
questions.explanation: find() returns the index of the first occurrence of the substring, which is 2 for 'l' in 'hello'.

questions.question: What is the output of 'Python'[1:4]?
questions.explanation: Slicing [1:4] returns characters from index 1 up to, but not including, index 4.

body.text: A list is an ordered, mutable collection that can store multiple items, including different data types, in a single variable.

body.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
mixed = [1, "two", 3.0, True]

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[0])    # apple
print(fruits[-1])   # cherry
print(fruits[0:2])  # ['apple', 'banana']

fruits[1] = "blueberry"
fruits.append("mango")     # add to end
fruits.insert(1, "kiwi")   # add at index
fruits.remove("apple")     # remove by value
fruits.pop()                # remove last item

rows: Adds item at a given index

body.code:
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[1:4])   # [20, 30, 40]
print(nums[:3])    # [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[::-1])  # reversed list

body.text: Lists are mutable, meaning their contents can be changed after creation, unlike strings and tuples.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a Python list?
questions.explanation: Lists are mutable (changeable) and maintain the order in which items were added.

questions.question: Which method adds an item to the end of a list?
questions.explanation: append() adds a single item to the end of the list.

questions.question: What does fruits.pop() do by default?
options: Removes and returns the last item
questions.explanation: Without an index argument, pop() removes and returns the last item in the list.

questions.question: What will nums[::-1] return for nums = [1,2,3]?
questions.explanation: A step of -1 in slicing reverses the entire list.

questions.question: Which method removes an item by its value rather than its index?
questions.explanation: remove() searches for and deletes the first item matching the given value.

questions.question: Can a Python list contain mixed data types?
options: Yes, a list can hold different data types
questions.explanation: Python lists can freely mix data types such as integers, strings, and booleans.

questions.question: Which method sorts a list in place?
questions.explanation: sort() rearranges the list's items in ascending order (by default) and modifies it directly.

questions.question: What is the result of len([10,20,30])?
questions.explanation: len() returns the number of items in the list, which is 3 here.

body.text: A tuple is an ordered collection similar to a list, but it is immutable, meaning its values cannot be changed after creation.

body.code:
point = (10, 20)
colors = ("red", "green", "blue")
single = (5,)   # comma required for a single-item tuple

colors = ("red", "green", "blue")
print(colors[0])    # red
print(colors[-1])   # blue
print(colors[0:2])  # ('red', 'green')

items: Data that should not change (constants, coordinates)
Faster than lists for fixed data
Can be used as dictionary keys (lists cannot)
Useful for returning multiple values from a function

body.code:
nums = (1, 2, 2, 3)
print(nums.count(2))   # 2
print(nums.index(3))   # 3

point = (10, 20)
x, y = point
print(x, y)   # 10 20

questions.question: What is the key difference between a list and a tuple?
options: Tuples can store more data types
Tuples are immutable while lists are mutable
questions.explanation: Unlike lists, tuples cannot be modified after they are created.

questions.question: How do you write a tuple with a single item, 5?
questions.explanation: A trailing comma is required to distinguish a single-item tuple from a parenthesized expression.

questions.question: Which symbol is used to define a tuple?
questions.explanation: Tuples are defined using parentheses, e.g. (1, 2, 3).

questions.question: What does tuple unpacking allow you to do?
options: Convert a tuple to a string
Assign tuple values to multiple variables at once
questions.explanation: Unpacking lets you assign each element of a tuple to a separate variable in one statement.

questions.question: Why might tuples be preferred over lists for fixed data?
options: They are immutable and slightly faster
questions.explanation: Because tuples cannot change, Python can optimize them, making them faster for constant data.

questions.question: Which method returns the number of times a value appears in a tuple?
questions.explanation: count() returns how many times a specified value appears in the tuple.

questions.question: Can a tuple be used as a dictionary key?
options: No, tuples can never be keys
Only if it has one element
questions.explanation: Since tuples are immutable and hashable, they can be used as dictionary keys, unlike lists.

questions.question: What is the output of: point = (10, 20); x, y = point; print(y)?
questions.explanation: Unpacking assigns 10 to x and 20 to y, so print(y) outputs 20.

body.text: A dictionary stores data as key-value pairs. Each key must be unique and is used to look up its corresponding value quickly.

body.code: student = {"name": "Alice", "age": 20, "grade": "A"}

print(student["name"])          # Alice
print(student.get("age"))       # 20
print(student.get("city", "N/A"))  # N/A (default if key missing)

student["city"] = "Chennai"     # add new key
student["age"] = 21             # update existing key

del student["grade"]
student.pop("city")

rows: Removes a key and returns its value

body.code:
for key, value in student.items():
    print(key, ":", value)

body.text: Dictionary keys must be unique and immutable (such as strings, numbers, or tuples); values can be any data type.

questions.question: What does a Python dictionary store?
questions.explanation: A dictionary maps unique keys to corresponding values.

questions.question: Which method safely retrieves a value without raising an error if the key is missing?
questions.explanation: get() returns None or a specified default instead of raising an error for a missing key.

questions.question: How do you add a new key-value pair to an existing dictionary?
questions.explanation: Assigning a value to a new key using square brackets adds it to the dictionary.

questions.question: Which method returns all key-value pairs of a dictionary?
questions.explanation: items() returns the dictionary's entries as key-value pairs.

questions.question: Can dictionary keys be duplicated?
options: No, each key must be unique
questions.explanation: Each key in a dictionary must be unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its value.

questions.question: Which data types can be used as dictionary keys?
options: Immutable types like strings, numbers, and tuples
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys must be immutable and hashable, so lists cannot be used as keys.

questions.question: What does student.pop("city") do?
options: Adds a new key called city
Removes the key 'city' and returns its value
questions.explanation: pop() removes the specified key from the dictionary and returns its associated value.

questions.question: How would you loop through both keys and values of a dictionary?
questions.explanation: Using dict.items() in a for loop gives access to both the key and value in each iteration.

body.text: A set is an unordered collection of unique items. Sets automatically remove duplicate values.

body.code:
fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}
nums = set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3])   # {1, 2, 3}

fruits.add("mango")
fruits.remove("banana")   # error if item not found
fruits.discard("kiwi")    # no error if item not found

items: Automatically remove duplicates from a collection
Fast membership testing (in operator)
Perform mathematical set operations easily
Unordered — items have no guaranteed order or index
Unique — duplicate values are automatically removed
Mutable — items can be added or removed, but the items themselves must be immutable

questions.question: What is the main characteristic of a set in Python?
options: Unordered and stores unique items only
questions.explanation: Sets automatically discard duplicate values and do not maintain a fixed order.

questions.question: What will set([1, 2, 2, 3]) produce?
questions.explanation: Converting a list to a set removes duplicate values, leaving {1, 2, 3}.

questions.question: Which method adds an item to a set without raising an error if it already exists?
questions.explanation: add() inserts an item into a set; if it already exists, nothing changes and no error occurs.

questions.question: What does a & b return for two sets a and b?
options: Only items common to both sets
questions.explanation: The & operator returns the intersection — items present in both sets.

questions.question: What is the difference between remove() and discard() on a set?
options: remove() raises an error if the item is missing, discard() does not
discard() raises an error, remove() does not
questions.explanation: remove() raises a KeyError for a missing item, while discard() silently does nothing.

questions.question: What does the | operator do between two sets?
questions.explanation: The | operator returns a union containing all unique items from both sets.

questions.question: Can a set contain duplicate values?
questions.explanation: Sets enforce uniqueness, so duplicate values are automatically eliminated.

questions.question: Which set operation returns items in set a but not in set b?
questions.explanation: The difference operation (a - b) returns elements found in a that are not in b.

body.text: A list comprehension is a concise way to create a new list by applying an expression to each item in an iterable, optionally with a condition.

body.code:
squares = [x**2 for x in range(5)]
print(squares)   # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

# Traditional loop
squares = []
for x in range(5):
    squares.append(x**2)

# List comprehension (equivalent, shorter)
squares = [x**2 for x in range(5)]

evens = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)   # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

labels = ["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in range(5)]
print(labels)   # ['even','odd','even','odd','even']

pairs = [(x, y) for x in range(2) for y in range(2)]
print(pairs)   # [(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)]

square_set = {x**2 for x in range(5)}
square_dict = {x: x**2 for x in range(5)}

body.text: List comprehensions are generally faster and more readable than equivalent for-loops for simple transformations, but very complex logic is often clearer as a regular loop.

questions.question: What does [x**2 for x in range(4)] produce?
questions.explanation: This comprehension squares each number from 0 to 3, giving [0, 1, 4, 9].

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a list comprehension?
options: It runs on a different interpreter
It creates lists in a more concise, readable way than a full loop
questions.explanation: List comprehensions let you build a list in a single, compact expression instead of several loop lines.

questions.question: What does [x for x in range(6) if x % 2 == 0] return?
questions.explanation: The if condition filters for even numbers only, giving [0, 2, 4].

questions.question: Can list comprehensions include an if-else expression for each item?
options: No, only filtering with if is allowed
Yes, using value_if_true if condition else value_if_false
questions.explanation: A comprehension can include a full conditional expression to choose between two output values.

questions.question: What type of brackets are used for a set comprehension?
questions.explanation: Curly braces {} are used for set comprehensions, similar to dictionary comprehensions.

questions.question: What does {x: x**2 for x in range(3)} create?
options: A dictionary mapping numbers to their squares
questions.explanation: This is a dictionary comprehension mapping each x to x squared, e.g. {0:0, 1:1, 2:4}.

questions.question: What does a nested list comprehension like [(x,y) for x in range(2) for y in range(2)] produce?
options: All combinations of x and y as tuples
questions.explanation: It behaves like nested for loops, producing all (x, y) combinations as tuples.

questions.question: When might a traditional for loop be preferred over a list comprehension?
options: When the logic is complex and a comprehension would hurt readability
questions.explanation: For complex, multi-step logic, a standard loop is often clearer than cramming everything into a comprehension.

body.text: 1. Recap: Choosing the Right Data Structure

body.code:
my_list = [1, 2, 2, 3]
my_set = set(my_list)      # {1, 2, 3}
my_tuple = tuple(my_list)  # (1, 2, 2, 3)
back_to_list = list(my_set)

body.text: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Functions help organize code, avoid repetition, and make programs easier to maintain.

body.text: A function without a return statement returns None by default.

questions.question: What does a function return if it has no return statement?

questions.question: Why are functions useful in programming?

body.text: Positional arguments are matched to parameters based on their order in the function call.
Keyword arguments are passed using the parameter name, so their order does not matter.

body.text: *args allows a function to accept any number of positional arguments, collected into a tuple.
**kwargs allows a function to accept any number of keyword arguments, collected into a dictionary.
Order matters when defining a function: regular parameters, then *args, then **kwargs.

questions.question: What does *args allow a function to accept?

questions.explanation: *args collects any number of extra positional arguments into a tuple.

questions.question: What does **kwargs collect its arguments into?

questions.question: In a function call, what determines a keyword argument?

questions.question: What would total(1, 2, 3) return if total is defined as def total(*args): return sum(args)?

questions.question: Which is true about combining *args and **kwargs in one function?

body.text: A lambda function is a small, anonymous function defined using the lambda keyword, typically used for short, one-time operations.

body.text: map() applies a given function to every item in an iterable and returns a map object (convert to list to view results).

body.text: filter() keeps only the items from an iterable for which a function returns True.

body.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

body.text: reduce(), found in the functools module, combines all items of an iterable into a single value using a function.

body.code:
from functools import reduce
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]

body.text: map, filter and reduce are core tools of functional-style programming in Python and are often paired with lambda functions.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to create an anonymous function in Python?

questions.question: What does map(function, iterable) do?

Applies the function to every item and returns the results

questions.question: What does filter(function, iterable) return?

questions.question: What is a key limitation of a lambda function compared to a regular function?

It cannot be assigned to a variable
questions.explanation: Lambda functions are restricted to a single expression and cannot include multiple statements.

questions.question: What will list(map(lambda x: x*2, [1,2,3])) produce?

questions.question: What does reduce(lambda a,b: a+b, [1,2,3,4]) return?

filter() offers a more concise, functional way to select matching items

body.text: A module is simply a Python file (.py) containing functions, variables, and classes that can be reused in other programs.

chapters.title: Day 19: Introduction to OOP - Classes and Objects

body.text: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming style that organizes code around objects, which bundle data (attributes) and behavior (methods) together.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects. It defines what attributes and methods the objects will have.

body.code:
s1 = Student("Alice", 20)
s2 = Student("Bob", 22)

s1.greet()   # Hi, I am Alice
print(s2.age)   # 22

rows: A special method called automatically when an object is created (constructor)
Refers to the current object instance; must be the first parameter of instance methods

items: Attributes: variables that belong to an object (e.g. self.name)
Methods: functions defined inside a class that describe an object's behavior

body.code:
class Car:
    wheels = 4   # class attribute (shared)

    def __init__(self, brand):
        self.brand = brand   # instance attribute (unique per object)

c1 = Car("Toyota")
c2 = Car("Honda")
print(c1.wheels, c1.brand)   # 4 Toyota
print(c2.wheels, c2.brand)   # 4 Honda

body.text: Every instance method in Python automatically receives the object itself as the first argument, conventionally named self.

questions.question: What does a class represent in OOP?
questions.explanation: A class defines the structure and behavior that its objects (instances) will share.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the __init__ method?
options: To automatically initialize a new object's attributes when it is created
questions.explanation: __init__ is the constructor, automatically called to set up a new object's initial state.

questions.question: What does 'self' refer to inside a class method?
questions.explanation: self refers to the specific object the method is being called on.

questions.question: How do you create an object (instance) of a class named Student?
questions.explanation: Calling the class name like a function, e.g. Student("Alice", 20), creates a new instance.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute?
options: Class attributes are shared by all instances; instance attributes are unique to each object
Instance attributes are shared by all objects
questions.explanation: Class attributes belong to the class and are shared, while instance attributes are set per object, usually in __init__.

questions.question: In class Student: def greet(self): ..., why must self be the first parameter?
options: It's optional and can be omitted
Python automatically passes the calling object as the first argument to instance methods
It refers to the class name
questions.explanation: Python implicitly passes the object itself as the first argument whenever an instance method is called.

questions.question: What is an object in OOP terms?
options: An instance of a class, with its own data
questions.explanation: An object is a concrete instance created from a class, holding its own attribute values.

questions.question: Given s1 = Student("Alice", 20), how would you access Alice's age?
questions.explanation: Dot notation, s1.age, accesses the age attribute stored on the s1 object.

body.text: Inheritance allows a class (child) to reuse the attributes and methods of another class (parent), promoting code reuse.
super() lets a child class call methods from its parent class, often used inside __init__ to reuse parent initialization logic.

rows: One child inherits from one parent
A child inherits from more than one parent class
A class inherits from a child class, forming a chain

body.text: Polymorphism means 'many forms' — the same method name can behave differently depending on the object that calls it.
When a child class defines a method with the same name as one in its parent, it overrides (replaces) the parent's version for that class.
Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship — a Dog is an Animal, a Cat is an Animal — allowing shared behavior with specialized differences.

questions.question: What does inheritance allow in OOP?
options: A class to remove another class's methods
A class to reuse attributes and methods from a parent class
Two classes to merge into one file
questions.explanation: Inheritance lets a child class access and reuse the parent class's attributes and methods.

questions.question: How is inheritance written in a class definition, e.g. Dog inheriting from Animal?
questions.explanation: Python specifies the parent class in parentheses after the child class name: class Dog(Animal):

questions.question: What does the super() function do?
options: Gives access to methods of the parent class from within the child class
Converts a child into a parent
questions.explanation: super() allows a child class to call and reuse the parent class's methods, such as __init__.

questions.question: What is polymorphism in OOP?
options: The ability for the same method name to behave differently across classes
A method that returns multiple values
questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows different classes to implement the same method name in their own way.

questions.question: What is method overriding?
options: Deleting a method from a class
A child class redefining a method that exists in its parent class
questions.explanation: Overriding occurs when a child class provides its own version of a method already defined in the parent.

questions.question: In class Dog(Animal): what is Animal called?
questions.explanation: Animal is the parent (or base/super) class that Dog inherits from.

questions.question: What relationship does inheritance typically model?
questions.explanation: Inheritance usually represents an 'is-a' relationship, such as 'a Dog is an Animal.'

questions.question: Given the Dog and Cat example both defining speak(), what happens when animal.speak() is called in a loop over both objects?
options: Each object calls its own overridden version of speak()
questions.explanation: Polymorphism ensures each object's own overridden speak() method executes, producing different output.

body.text: Encapsulation means bundling data and the methods that operate on it within a class, while restricting direct access to some of an object's internal details.

rows: Intended for internal use, accessible but discouraged outside the class
Name-mangled, harder to access directly from outside the class

items: Protects internal state from accidental modification
Allows validation logic when data changes (e.g., in deposit)
Hides implementation details from the user of the class

body.text: Special methods, surrounded by double underscores, let objects work with Python's built-in syntax like print(), len(), and +.
Dunder methods are what allow custom objects to integrate naturally with Python's built-in functions and operators.

questions.question: What is encapsulation in OOP?
options: Bundling data and methods together while restricting direct access to internal details
Creating multiple objects from a class
Converting a class into a function
questions.explanation: Encapsulation groups data and behavior together and controls access to an object's internals.

questions.question: What does a double underscore prefix (e.g. __balance) suggest about an attribute?
options: It is intended to be private and is name-mangled
questions.explanation: Double underscore attributes are treated as private by convention, using Python's name mangling.

questions.question: What does the __str__ method control?
options: What is displayed when print() is called on an object
How the object is compared to others
questions.explanation: __str__ defines the readable string representation shown when the object is printed.

questions.question: Which special method allows len(obj) to work on a custom object?
questions.explanation: Defining __len__ in a class lets Python's built-in len() function work on its objects.

questions.question: Why is a deposit() method used instead of setting balance directly in the Account example?
options: It allows validation, such as rejecting negative amounts, before changing the balance
It is required by Python syntax
questions.explanation: A method can check conditions like amount > 0 before applying a change, protecting data integrity.

questions.question: What are 'dunder' methods named after?
options: Double underscores surrounding the method name
questions.explanation: 'Dunder' is short for 'double underscore', referring to the __method__ naming pattern.

questions.question: Which special method would you define to customize how the + operator works between two custom objects?
questions.explanation: __add__ lets you define custom behavior for the + operator on instances of your class.

questions.question: What is a benefit of restricting direct access to an object's attributes?
options: It makes the program run in a different language
It protects internal state and allows controlled, validated changes
It removes the need for methods
questions.explanation: Restricting direct access lets the class enforce rules and prevent invalid or unsafe modifications.

units.title: Week 4: File Handling, Exceptions & Advanced Topics

chapters.title: Day 23: File Handling - Reading and Writing Files

body.text: File handling lets a program read data from files and save data to files, so information persists after the program ends.

body.code:
file = open("notes.txt", "r")   # open for reading
content = file.read()
file.close()

rows: Read (default); error if file doesn't exist
Write; creates file or overwrites existing content
Append; adds to the end of the file
Create; error if file already exists

body.text: The with statement automatically closes the file, even if an error occurs, so it is the recommended way to work with files.

body.code:
with open("notes.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
print(content)
# file is automatically closed here

with open("notes.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Hello, this is a note.\n")
    file.write("Second line.")

rows: Reads the entire file as a string
Reads all lines into a list
Writes a string to the file

body.text: Using 'w' mode overwrites the entire file — use 'a' mode if you want to preserve existing content and add to it.

questions.question: Which mode opens a file for reading only?

body.text: An exception is an error that occurs during program execution. If not handled, it stops the program and shows an error message (traceback).

body.code: print(10 / 0)   # ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

body.text: The try block contains code that might raise an error; the except block defines how to handle that error without crashing the program.

rows: Only if the try block completes with no exception
Always runs, whether or not an exception occurred
Invalid value for an operation, e.g. int('abc')
Opening a file that doesn't exist

questions.question: What is the purpose of a try-except block?

questions.explanation: try-except lets a program gracefully handle errors instead of stopping abruptly.

questions.question: When does the else clause in a try-except-else block execute?

Only if the try block completes successfully with no exception

Only when there is an error
Always, regardless of whether an exception occurred

questions.question: How do you manually trigger (raise) an exception in Python?

questions.question: What does 'except Exception as e' do?

body.text: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight, text-based format used to store and exchange data. It maps naturally to Python dictionaries and lists.
Python's built-in json module converts between JSON text and Python objects.

body.code:
import json

data = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}
json_string = json.dumps(data)
print(json_string)   # '{"name": "Alice", "age": 25}'

json_string = '{"name": "Alice", "age": 25}'
data = json.loads(json_string)
print(data["name"])   # Alice

import json

# Writing to a file
with open("data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"score": 90}, f)

# Reading from a file
with open("data.json", "r") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
print(data["score"])

body.text: JSON keys must be strings, and JSON does not support Python-specific types like tuples or sets directly.

questions.question: What does JSON stand for?
questions.explanation: JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation, a common data-interchange format.

questions.question: Which function converts a Python dictionary into a JSON string?
questions.explanation: json.dumps() serializes a Python object into a JSON-formatted string.

questions.question: Which function converts a JSON string into a Python object?
questions.explanation: json.loads() parses a JSON string and returns the corresponding Python object.

concept.title: Regular Expressions with the re Module

body.text: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern used to search, match, or manipulate text based on specific rules.

body.code: import re

rows: One or more of the preceding character
Zero or more of the preceding character

body.code:
import re

text = "My phone number is 98765"
match = re.search(r"\d+", text)
if match:
    print(match.group())   # 98765

text = "Order 5 apples and 10 bananas"
numbers = re.findall(r"\d+", text)
print(numbers)   # ['5', '10']

text = "My number is 98765"
masked = re.sub(r"\d+", "XXXXX", text)
print(masked)   # My number is XXXXX

body.text: Regular expressions are powerful for validation and text extraction, but overly complex patterns can be hard to read — comment or document them when possible.

options: A list of all number sequences found in the text
questions.explanation: findall() returns a list of all non-overlapping matches of the pattern in the string.

questions.explanation: re.sub() substitutes all matches of a pattern with a specified replacement string.

options: One or more repetitions of the preceding character
questions.explanation: + requires at least one occurrence of the preceding character or group.

questions.explanation: The ^ symbol anchors a pattern to the beginning of the string.

options: They make code run without errors
They allow flexible searching, matching, and validating of text patterns
They are required to import files
questions.explanation: Regex provides a powerful, flexible way to search, validate, and manipulate text based on patterns.

chapters.title: Day 27: Working with Date and Time

body.text: 1. Why Work with Dates and Times?
Many programs need to record timestamps, calculate durations, or format dates for display — Python's datetime module handles all of this.

body.code: import datetime

body.text: 2. Getting the Current Date and Time

body.code:
import datetime

now = datetime.datetime.now()
print(now)             # e.g. 2026-08-04 10:15:30.123456

today = datetime.date.today()
print(today)           # e.g. 2026-08-04

d = datetime.date(2026, 1, 15)
print(d)   # 2026-01-15

now = datetime.datetime.now()
print(now.strftime("%d-%m-%Y"))     # 04-08-2026
print(now.strftime("%H:%M:%S"))     # 10:15:30

body.text: 5. Parsing a String into a Date with strptime()

body.code:
date_str = "15-01-2026"
parsed = datetime.datetime.strptime(date_str, "%d-%m-%Y")
print(parsed)

from datetime import date, timedelta

today = date.today()
next_week = today + timedelta(days=7)
print(next_week)

body.text: strftime() converts a date object to a formatted string; strptime() does the reverse, parsing a string into a date object.

chapters.title: Day 28: Introduction to NumPy and Pandas

body.text: NumPy and Pandas are widely used third-party libraries for numerical computing and data analysis, forming the foundation of Python's data science ecosystem.

body.code: pip install numpy pandas

body.text: NumPy's core feature is the ndarray, an efficient, fixed-type array that supports fast mathematical operations.

body.code:
import numpy as np

arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(arr * 2)          # [2 4 6 8]
print(arr.mean())       # 2.5
print(arr.shape)        # (4,)

zeros = np.zeros(3)       # [0. 0. 0.]
ones = np.ones((2, 2))    # 2x2 array of ones
range_arr = np.arange(0, 10, 2)   # [0 2 4 6 8]

body.text: Pandas provides two main structures: Series (a labeled 1-D array) and DataFrame (a labeled 2-D table), ideal for handling tabular data.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

data = {"Name": ["Alice", "Bob"], "Age": [25, 30]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)

body.text: NumPy is optimized for numerical arrays and math, while Pandas builds on it to handle labeled, tabular data like spreadsheets and CSV files.

concept.title: Virtual Environments, pip, and Debugging Basics

body.text: A virtual environment is an isolated Python setup that keeps a project's dependencies separate from other projects and the system-wide Python installation.

items: Avoid version conflicts between different projects
Keep the system Python installation clean
Make it easy to share a project's exact dependencies

body.text: 3. Creating and Using a Virtual Environment

body.code:
python -m venv myenv

# Activate on Windows
myenv\Scripts\activate

# Activate on macOS/Linux
source myenv/bin/activate

# Deactivate
deactivate

pip freeze > requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt

rows: Quickly check variable values at different points
Identify the exact line and type of error
Using a debugger (e.g. pdb, IDE breakpoints)
Step through code line by line
Check that a condition holds true during development

body.code:
import pdb

def divide(a, b):
    pdb.set_trace()   # execution pauses here for inspection
    return a / b

body.text: A traceback shows the sequence of function calls leading to an error, ending with the exact error type and message — always read it from the bottom up first.
Good debugging habits, like isolating the problem and checking assumptions with print() or assert, save far more time than guessing.
